items.passage: What do you say to someone who left without a word and comes back the same way? I asked myself that at the bus depot in Gdansk, where my brother Marcus and I had gone to meet Zofia, our cousin, eleven years after she boarded a coach to Berlin. Marcus had polished his shoes; I had not. Our shop sold fewer radios each month, and he talked about it on the drive as if Zofia might bring customers in her suitcase. She stepped down carrying one small bag and kissed us both, and she explained nothing. I waited for an apology that never came and was surprised to find I did not need it. Watching her laugh at Marcus's terrible jokes, I thought the years had cost her more than they had cost us. A cleaner moved between the empty bays, pushing a wide broom over oil stains shaped like countries.

Anacleto,
I am writing from the projection booth, where the old machine still smells of oil and dust even though no film has run through it since spring. Your father's plane arrived this morning, wrapped in a flour sack, with a note saying he wished me to have it. I know you expected it. You swept his shop for six years before I ever held a chisel, and I have seen you run your thumb along that blade as if greeting someone. I will use it, because refusing a dead man's gift seems worse than accepting it badly. But every board I smooth will be a board I owe you, and I mean to keep the account. Tell your mother the booth's door finally closes; I rehung it on Tuesday with new hinges.
Cleotilde

items.passage: Three rules for lessons, Grandfather Kerem says: no English, no dictionary, no laughing at his handwriting. Tonight we broke all three in the boarding-house kitchen while the kettle muttered on the stove. I had found the letter last week inside his old grammar book, addressed to a woman named only by an initial, and I asked him to teach me enough to read it myself. He agreed too quickly. Tonight he made me copy one sentence about the sea eleven times, and when I finally read it aloud, he turned toward the window and said my vowels were still too round. I think he is glad someone will understand it at last, and afraid of exactly the same thing. A neighbor's cat slept on the bread bin again; tomorrow I must buy more sugar.

items.passage: Once, in a cabin buried to its windowsills in Tromso snow, a young cook named Emil received a gift from his stern uncle Silas: a pair of fine leather gloves, two sizes too small. Emil thanked him warmly and wore them to stir the porridge, though his knuckles pressed white against the seams. For a week he praised their softness, and for a week Silas watched him fumble the ladle. On the eighth morning, Silas set a second pair beside the stove, wide and plain and lined with wool, and said nothing at all. Emil put them on and, for the first time all week, laughed. In the old telling, the two of them then shoveled a path to the woodpile while the northern sky went green above the drifts.

items.passage: "Same as always?" Shamsuddin asked, and Danish nodded, which was most of their conversation for the afternoon. Every Thursday for forty years, the two men had come back to the music room of the Karachi school where they had once been students, to tune its tired harmonium and dust the tabla skins. Neither was paid. Neither, as far as I ever saw, suggested stopping. As a boy I sat on the bench and watched them work, my grandfather pressing keys while his friend adjusted reeds, and I thought them dull. Only later did I notice how each corrected note seemed to answer the one before, like a sentence the other could finish. When Danish died, Shamsuddin came the next Thursday alone and tuned the instrument to the same pitch. Afterward the room was locked, and the key hung on a nail in the headmaster's office.

Dear Fumiko,
I lost again. You will be pleased, though you will pretend otherwise when we meet at the club. I am writing from a train compartment somewhere in Hokkaido, with our travel set balanced on my knees, replaying the endgame you won on Sunday. For twelve years we have played every week, and for twelve years neither of us has mentioned the tournament in Osaka or the move you swear you did not take back. I used to think our silence was cowardice. Lately I suspect it is the only reason we still sit across from each other. The snow here has buried the fences entirely; only the tops of the telegraph poles mark the road.
Yours in rivalry,
Rukhsana

Three rules for the hive, Siti said:
move slowly, breathe low, never curse in the yard.
Mandla, her clerk through twenty years of verdicts,
held the smoker that had been her husband's,
its leather bellows patched with his careful thread.

She did not weep. She lifted a frame
heavy with gold, and the bees walked over her wrist
like a sentence she had finally learned to read.

Once, his name caught in her throat
and the yard went quiet for a breath.
Then the smoke rose again, gray and sweet,
and Mandla pumped it the way she showed him,
slow, slow, the hum returning
to the longan trees along the fence.

### lit40-medium-01-015 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 main_idea_or_purpose · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 곳의 근거를 합쳐 요지를 잡아야 하고, 오답 하나는 일화 요약에 그치는 부분 요지다
